blocks.content: The Database Fundamentals module covered what databases are and how they are actually built. This new module, SQL Fundamentals, gets hands on with the actual language you use to talk to a relational database, starting with SELECT, the statement that asks the database for specific columns of data.

SELECT is genuinely the most common SQL statement you will ever write, and understanding it precisely, not just enough to get by, is the foundation everything else in this SQL Fundamentals module, and the modules that follow it, is built on.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784032857892-905793519.png
blocks.alt: SQL SELECT opens the SQL Fundamentals module by asking the database for specific columns of data

blocks.content: 1. What SELECT Actually Does

A SELECT statement names which columns you actually want back from the database, rather than every piece of data that exists. It also names which table to read those columns from, since a real database typically holds many tables.

The database returns rows matching your request, in an order the database chooses internally unless you explicitly tell it otherwise, a detail worth remembering, since assuming a specific row order without asking for it is a genuinely common mistake covered later in this topic.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784032859718-677453915.png
blocks.alt: SELECT names which columns you want, which table to read them from, and returns matching rows in an order the database chooses unless told otherwise

blocks.content: 2. The Anatomy of a Basic SELECT
blocks.text: 2. The Anatomy of a Basic SELECT

blocks.content: A basic SELECT has a genuinely simple structure. SELECT, followed by the columns you actually want, separated by commas if there is more than one. FROM, followed by the table those columns actually live in.
And a semicolon, ending the statement, a convention worth following consistently even though some tools tolerate its absence for a single statement.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784032862647-512626861.png
blocks.alt: The anatomy of a basic SELECT: the columns you want, the table they live in, and a semicolon ending the statement

3. SELECT Star Versus Explicit Columns

SELECT star, using an asterisk instead of naming columns, returns every column in the table, which is genuinely convenient while exploring data interactively at a terminal, since you do not have to know the exact column names in advance.

SELECT with explicitly named columns takes a little more typing, but is genuinely safer and clearer in real application code, since it makes obvious exactly what data the query actually depends on, rather than silently depending on every column that happens to exist right now.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784032864181-779223551.png
blocks.alt: SELECT star returns every column, convenient for exploration but genuinely risky in application code; explicit named columns are slower to write but genuinely safer

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.content: Using SELECT star in real, production application code out of habit or convenience. This works fine until someone adds a new column to the table, at which point your application may suddenly receive data it never expected.
4. A Worked Example
A concrete table shows this applied. A table named employees holds many columns, id, name, department, salary, hire date, and more, but a specific query only actually needs two of them.
SELECT name, department FROM employees;

This query returns only the name and department columns, for every single row in the employees table, ignoring every other column that exists, even though those other columns are still genuinely there in the underlying table.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784032867042-494239119.png
blocks.alt: A worked example: a table with many columns, and a query selecting only name and department, returning just those two columns for every row

blocks.content: 5. Why Explicit Columns Genuinely Matter

A few real, practical reasons explicit column selection matters in production code. A new column added to the table later does not silently break your application, since your query already named exactly what it needs, and simply ignores anything new. Less data is transferred over the network too, since you are only pulling the specific columns you actually use, which is genuinely faster, especially over many rows.

And the query itself documents exactly what data it actually needs, a real, practical benefit for anyone reading the code later, including your future self, who no longer has to guess which of the table many columns actually matter for this specific query.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784032868963-378179174.png
blocks.alt: Explicit columns mean a new column added later will not silently break your application, less data transfers over the network, and the query documents its own real needs

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: SELECT star is genuinely fine, and often faster to write, while exploring data interactively. The real risk is specifically in application code that runs repeatedly in production, where an unexpected new column can silently change behavior.
6. Genuinely Common Mistakes

A few real patterns undermine SELECT usage. Using SELECT star in real application code purely out of habit, rather than a deliberate choice, missing the real risk covered above. Forgetting that the table genuinely must already exist before you can select from it, a query against a nonexistent table simply fails with a clear error.

And assuming row order is guaranteed without an explicit ORDER BY clause, which is covered as its own dedicated topic shortly, since a database is genuinely free to return rows in whatever order is most convenient for it internally, unless you explicitly ask for a specific order.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784032871664-37272464.png
blocks.alt: Common mistakes: SELECT star out of habit in application code, forgetting a table must exist first, and assuming row order without an explicit ORDER BY

8. Common Mistakes

items: Writing SELECT star in application code without a real reason: risks unexpectedly receiving new columns added to the table later.
Assuming returned rows are in a specific, meaningful order: row order is never guaranteed without an explicit ORDER BY clause.
Selecting columns you do not actually use in your application: wastes real network bandwidth transferring data nobody will use.
